title: Classical Conditioning
description: Pavlov's dogs and the mechanics of stimulus association

concepts.title: Pavlov and the Salivary Reflex
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 1890s the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying the digestive system of dogs when he noticed something unexpected: his dogs began salivating not only when food touched their tongues, but also at the sight of the lab assistant who fed them, or the sound of approaching footsteps.

Pavlov realised this was a form of learning, and he set out to map it systematically. He paired a neutral stimulus — a metronome or bell — with the presentation of meat powder. After repeated pairings, the bell alone produced salivation.

The vocabulary he developed is still used today:

UCS (unconditioned stimulus): the meat — naturally elicits a response.
UCR (unconditioned response): salivation to meat — innate.
CS (conditioned stimulus): the bell — initially neutral.
CR (conditioned response): salivation to the bell alone — learned.

Pavlov won the 1904 Nobel Prize for the digestive work, but his discovery of associative learning reshaped psychology far more profoundly.

concepts.title: Acquisition, Extinction, and Spontaneous Recovery
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical conditioning unfolds in predictable phases.

Acquisition: the CS and UCS are repeatedly paired, and the CR strengthens. Timing matters — the CS must reliably precede the UCS by a short interval. Simultaneous or backward pairings produce weak learning.

Extinction: if the CS is later presented many times without the UCS, the CR gradually fades. The dog stops salivating to a bell that no longer predicts food.

Spontaneous recovery: after a rest period, presenting the CS again often elicits a partial CR — extinction does not erase the original learning, it suppresses it. This shows that the original association is preserved beneath the extinction-trained inhibition.

Pavlov also demonstrated generalisation (similar tones elicit the CR) and discrimination (animals can be trained to respond only to a specific tone, ignoring others). These four processes — acquisition, extinction, recovery, generalisation — apply across species and stimulus types.

concepts.title: Watson and Little Albert
concepts.contentHtml:
John B. Watson founded American behaviourism with his 1913 manifesto, declaring that psychology should abandon introspection and study only observable behaviour. Mind, for Watson, was a black box; what mattered was the relationship between stimulus and response.

To show that human emotions could be conditioned, Watson and Rosalie Rayner ran the now-infamous Little Albert experiment in 1920. They presented an 11-month-old infant with a white rat (initially neutral). Each time Albert reached for the rat, they struck a steel bar behind his head with a hammer, producing a startling crash.

After only seven pairings, Albert cried at the mere sight of the rat. The fear generalised to a rabbit, a fur coat, and a Santa Claus mask — all white and furry. Watson took this as evidence that phobias are conditioned, not innate.

The study would not pass any modern ethics board: Albert was never deconditioned, and his identity and fate remain debated. But its theoretical influence — that emotional life is built up from learned associations — was enormous.

title: Operant Conditioning
description: Thorndike, Skinner, and behaviour shaped by consequences

concepts.title: Thorndike's Law of Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
Before Skinner there was Edward Thorndike, whose Columbia dissertation (1898) introduced the puzzle box. A hungry cat was placed in a slatted crate; pulling a loop of string opened the door and gave access to fish outside.

The first escape was almost accidental — the cat thrashed, scratched, and eventually triggered the latch. But over successive trials, the time-to-escape dropped sharply. The cat had not solved the box by insight; it had been shaped by its consequences.

From these data Thorndike formulated the Law of Effect: responses followed by satisfying consequences are more likely to recur in the same situation; responses followed by discomfort become less likely.

This is the founding principle of all consequence-based learning theory. Where Pavlov's dog learned that a stimulus predicts something, Thorndike's cat learned that an action produces something. The distinction — between Pavlovian (classical) and instrumental (operant) learning — would organise the next century of research.

concepts.title: Skinner: Reinforcement and Punishment
concepts.contentHtml:
B.F. Skinner took Thorndike's law and built an experimental empire around it. His operant chamber (the 'Skinner box') let a pigeon or rat freely emit responses — pecking a key, pressing a lever — while consequences were precisely controlled.

Skinner distinguished four basic operations along two axes: add or remove a stimulus by increase or decrease in behaviour:

Positive reinforcement: add something pleasant (food pellet) — behaviour increases.
Negative reinforcement: remove something aversive (loud noise stops) — behaviour increases.
Positive punishment: add something aversive (shock) — behaviour decreases.
Negative punishment: remove something pleasant (lose tokens) — behaviour decreases.

Note that 'negative' does not mean 'bad' — it just means 'subtractive'. Negative reinforcement strengthens behaviour by ending an unpleasant state, which is why fastening a seatbelt to silence the warning chime gets reinforced. Confusion between negative reinforcement and punishment is one of the most common errors in introductory psychology.

concepts.title: Schedules of Reinforcement
concepts.contentHtml:
Skinner discovered that when reinforcement is delivered matters as much as whether it is delivered. He and Charles Ferster catalogued four basic schedules, each producing a distinctive response pattern:

Fixed Ratio (FR): reinforce after every n responses (e.g. piecework wages). High response rates with a brief post-reinforcement pause.
Variable Ratio (VR): reinforce after a variable number of responses, averaging n. Extremely high, steady rates — and remarkably resistant to extinction. This is the engine of slot machines and social-media feeds.
Fixed Interval (FI): reinforce the first response after t seconds. Produces a 'scallop' — responding accelerates as the interval ends.
Variable Interval (VI): reinforce the first response after a variable time, averaging t. Steady, moderate, persistent responding.

Variable schedules produce behaviour that is far more durable than continuous reinforcement, because the learner cannot tell when the next payoff will arrive. Shaping — reinforcing successive approximations to a target behaviour — leverages these schedules to teach complex skills, from pigeon ping-pong to circus tricks.

title: Cracks in the Behaviourist Programme
description: Tolman's maps, Garcia's nausea, and the limits of stimulus-response

concepts.title: Tolman's Cognitive Maps
concepts.contentHtml:
Edward Tolman was a behaviourist by training but a quiet rebel by temperament. In a series of maze experiments at Berkeley in the 1930s and 1940s, he showed that rats learn things behaviourists said they could not.

In his famous latent learning studies (Tolman & Honzik, 1930), one group of rats explored a maze for ten days with no food reward. According to strict reinforcement theory, they should have learned nothing. But when food was suddenly introduced on day 11, these rats raced to the goal almost as quickly as a group that had been rewarded all along.

The rats had learned the maze without reinforcement; the reward only revealed that learning. Tolman concluded that animals build internal cognitive maps — spatial representations of their environment — and that learning is not reducible to stimulus-response habits.

This was heresy in 1948. But Tolman's work, ignored for decades, anticipated the cognitive revolution and is now vindicated by the discovery of place cells and grid cells in the hippocampus.

concepts.title: Bandura and the Bobo Doll
concepts.contentHtml:
Albert Bandura argued that humans (and many animals) learn not only from direct reinforcement but from observation. His 1961 Bobo doll experiment at Stanford became one of the most cited studies in psychology.

Children watched an adult interact with a five-foot inflatable Bobo doll. In one condition the adult attacked it — punching, kicking, sitting on it, shouting 'Pow!' In a control condition the adult played quietly. The children were then mildly frustrated and left alone with toys including the Bobo doll.

The children who had watched the aggressive model imitated specific attacks they had never directly performed or been rewarded for. Critically, they had received no reinforcement for aggression — they had simply observed it.

Bandura's social learning theory (later social cognitive theory) added four cognitive components missing from strict behaviourism: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. The learner has to notice the model, encode the act, be able to perform it, and have reason to do so. Behaviour, Bandura insisted, is the product of person, environment, and cognition reciprocally — not stimulus and response alone.

concepts.title: The Garcia Effect and Biological Constraints
concepts.contentHtml:
Strict behaviourism assumed that any stimulus could be conditioned to any response with equal ease — the 'principle of equipotentiality'. John Garcia demolished this in a series of studies on rats in the 1950s and 1960s.

Garcia and Koelling (1966) gave rats flavoured water paired with one of two punishments: a flash-and-click, or X-ray-induced nausea hours later. They also tested water signalled by a noise-light combination paired with the same punishments.

The result was striking: rats associated taste with nausea — even with delays of hours — but failed to associate taste with shock. Conversely they associated noise-light with shock, but not with nausea. Some pairings were learned in a single trial; others could not be learned at all.

This is preparedness: evolution has biased organisms to learn ecologically relevant associations. A rat that gets sick remembers what it ate, not what it heard. Behaviourism's central assumption — that minds are blank associative machines — was untenable. Biology shapes what can be learned.

title: Modelling Associative Learning
description: The Rescorla-Wagner model and the cognitive revolution

concepts.title: Surprise and the Rescorla-Wagner Model
concepts.contentHtml:
By the late 1960s it was clear that simple temporal pairing of CS and UCS could not explain everything. Robert Rescorla showed that what really mattered was whether the CS provided information about the UCS — whether it predicted the UCS better than chance.

In Rescorla's contingency studies, two groups received the same number of CS-UCS pairings. But one group also received the UCS at random times in the absence of the CS. That group did not learn. The CS was redundant; it predicted nothing new.

This insight became the Rescorla-Wagner model (1972), still the workhorse of associative learning theory. It says that learning happens when there is prediction error: the difference between what was expected and what occurred. When a UCS is fully predicted, learning stops, even if pairings continue.

The model elegantly explains blocking: if a CS already predicts the UCS, adding a second CS in compound produces no learning to the new cue, because there is no surprise left to drive it. Decades later, dopamine neurons in the midbrain were found to encode exactly this prediction-error signal.

concepts.title: The Cognitive Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1960s, behaviourism's grip on academic psychology was loosening. Several converging blows did the work.

Chomsky's review (1959) of Skinner's Verbal Behavior argued that the productivity and structure of human language could not be explained by reinforcement histories. Children produce sentences they have never heard and could not have been rewarded for.

Computers made the idea of internal representation respectable again — minds, like machines, could process symbols. Miller's 'magical number seven' (1956) put working memory back at the centre of the field.

Bandura, Tolman, and Garcia had each shown specific phenomena that strict S-R theory could not handle. And Festinger's cognitive dissonance work showed that humans care about consistency between their beliefs in ways that defy simple drive reduction.

What emerged was not a rejection of learning theory but its enrichment. The cognitive revolution put internal states — representations, expectations, memories, plans — back into the explanatory toolkit, while keeping the rigorous experimental methods that behaviourism had bequeathed.

concepts.title: What Behaviourism Got Right
concepts.contentHtml:
It is easy to caricature behaviourism as a failed ideology. In fact much of its empirical content is solid, well-replicated science.

Classical and operant conditioning are real, robust phenomena that occur in nearly every species tested, from sea slugs to humans. The schedules of reinforcement Skinner described are mathematically precise and predictive. The mechanisms identified by the Rescorla-Wagner model are now grounded in well-characterised neural circuits.

Even more importantly, behaviourists insisted on operational definitions and objective measurement. They taught psychology to distrust loose introspective reports and to specify what would count as evidence. That methodological inheritance is universal in psychology now, even among researchers who study consciousness and cognition.

The mistake was not the data but the radical claim — that all explanation must terminate in stimulus and response, with nothing in between. That claim is gone. But the patient experimental analysis of behaviour remains a foundation for clinical psychology, neuroscience, and machine learning's reinforcement-learning algorithms alike.

title: Behaviourism Applied
description: From token economies to behaviour therapy and beyond

concepts.title: Behaviour Therapy and Systematic Desensitisation
concepts.contentHtml:
If phobias are conditioned, perhaps they can be deconditioned. Mary Cover Jones demonstrated this with a frightened toddler called Peter as early as 1924, gradually pairing a feared rabbit with milk and biscuits until the fear faded.

Joseph Wolpe formalised the technique in the 1950s as systematic desensitisation. The patient learns deep muscle relaxation, builds a hierarchy of fear-evoking situations from mild to extreme, and works up the hierarchy while remaining relaxed. Relaxation is incompatible with anxiety; through repeated pairing the CS (the spider, the elevator, the audience) loses its power.

Variants followed: flooding (immediate full exposure, no escape), exposure and response prevention for OCD, in vivo exposure for agoraphobia. These techniques, now subsumed under cognitive behavioural therapy, have the strongest empirical support of any psychotherapeutic methods for anxiety disorders.

Behaviour therapy is one of the clearest cases where laboratory learning theory translated directly into a humane and effective clinical practice — millions of treated patients owe a debt to Pavlov's dogs.

concepts.title: Applied Behaviour Analysis and Token Economies
concepts.contentHtml:
Applied Behaviour Analysis (ABA) emerged in the 1960s as the systematic application of operant principles to socially significant behaviour. Ivar Lovaas's work on autism and Sidney Bijou's on developmental disabilities are early landmarks.

A core ABA technique is the token economy, pioneered by Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin in psychiatric wards in the 1960s. Patients earned tokens for adaptive behaviours — making the bed, attending therapy, social interaction — and exchanged tokens for privileges. The tokens functioned as a generalised secondary reinforcer, flexible across situations and immediate enough to bridge the delay between behaviour and ultimate reward.

Token economies have since been used in classrooms, prisons, residential treatment, and weight-loss programmes. They work, but they raise enduring questions: do they produce internal motivation, or merely compliance that fades when tokens stop? Do they undermine intrinsic interest in tasks that are already rewarding?

Modern ABA is itself contested — autistic self-advocates have raised serious ethical objections to early intensive interventions — illustrating that even well-grounded techniques carry social and ethical weight beyond their efficacy data.

concepts.title: The Lasting Legacy
concepts.contentHtml:
Look around and the descendants of behaviourism are everywhere.

Reinforcement learning in artificial intelligence — the algorithms behind game-playing systems and recommendation engines — is essentially Thorndike's law of effect formalised. The temporal-difference learning rule used by these systems is mathematically related to the Rescorla-Wagner model.

Habit formation research applies operant principles to the design of products, public health interventions, and educational software. The streak counters and notification cues in apps are deliberate variable-ratio schedules, often to the user's detriment.

Animal training — from guide dogs to service primates to dolphin shows — relies almost entirely on positive reinforcement and shaping, the methods Skinner pioneered. Clicker training is a textbook secondary reinforcer.

Clinical psychology retains exposure-based therapies, contingency management for substance use, and parent-training programmes for children, all rooted in conditioning research.

Radical behaviourism lost the battle for psychology's soul. But the patient analysis of how environments shape behaviour, and behaviour shapes environments, has quietly won a thousand smaller victories — and remains indispensable wherever we want to change what creatures, including ourselves, do.
